note.question: How do competing crowdsourcing contests distort prizes and solver entry, and when can a platform improve welfare by coordinating budgets or recommending where solvers participate?
note.overview: Two firms simultaneously design prize allocations to attract solvers, and solvers then noncooperatively select at most one contest and exert costly effort. The paper derives symmetric participation-effort and upstream prize equilibria and studies platform budget restrictions and self-enforcing nudges.

components.label: Model sequence and system structure
components.explanation: Firms simultaneously commit to prize allocations. Solvers then simultaneously choose at most one contest and effort without observing how many others will enter. Submission quality is realized and prizes are paid by rank; platform interventions precede or shape these decisions. Firms compete for a common pool of solvers through prize schedules.

components.label: Contract equilibrium with upstream pure-strategy prize allocation and downstream solver participation-effort equilibrium
components.explanation: The model's equilibrium concept is Contract equilibrium with upstream pure-strategy prize allocation and downstream solver participation-effort equilibrium. Section 3 explicitly calls the nested game a contract equilibrium. Proposition 1 proves existence of a symmetric participation equilibrium with pure effort for 0<=vartheta<=vartheta*. Theorem 2 establishes existence of a pure prize-allocation equilibrium (not general uniqueness); winner-take-all is unique under the stated IFR condition. Theorem 5 gives a symmetric pure-strategy threshold equilibrium for ability-driven entry, unique within that class up to a measure-zero set.
